opus-5.5.text:
I think the two are really inseparable. From the outside, people sometimes see it as one bold decision: "Okay, we're going to train a trillion-parameter model." But internally it didn't feel like a single leap. The decision only became reasonable because a lot of preparation had already been done, often for quite different reasons at the time.

The way I see it, you can't decide to scale up on conviction alone. You have to ask: if we put this much compute and this much of the team's time into one run, what's the probability it actually works? That probability depends almost entirely on the technical groundwork. Do you have an optimizer you trust at that scale? Do you understand the training dynamics well enough that you won't hit instabilities halfway through and waste weeks? Is your data pipeline mature enough, especially on the token-efficiency side, given that high-quality data is becoming the real constraint rather than compute?

A lot of what we worked on before K2 answered those questions. When we explored a different optimizer, for example, the motivation was quite fundamental: if data is limited, how do you get more intelligence out of each token? That started as research, not as "we need this for K2." But once we saw it held up at larger scales, and we found ways to deal with problems like training instability, it changed our calculation. Something that would have looked too risky became something we could reasonably bet on.

So the order is a bit subtle. The preparation isn't just execution after the decision. It's what makes the decision possible. And once you decide, the decision also feeds back. It forces you to prioritize, to cut things that don't matter, and to really industrialize the parts that were still somewhat experimental.

There's also the agentic side. We felt the next important capability wasn't only chatting well. It was the model taking actions, using tools, working through long tasks. That shaped the data and post-training preparation a lot. K2 was the point where we felt the base-model technology and our view of what the model should do had come together enough to commit.

If I had to sum it up, I'd say the decision is a bet, but a good bet is one where you've already reduced the uncertainty as much as you can. The technical preparation is how you earn the right to make that bet.

r001.rationale: The response says prior technical preparation made the K2 decision possible, but it does not state that training K2 within two or three months would be infeasible if the groundwork began only after the decision.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as two things that had to converge, and neither one alone would have been enough.

The decision itself was actually fairly simple once we were honest with ourselves. By the second half of last year it was clear that the scaling path toward AGI runs through large-scale pre-training plus reinforcement learning, and that if we wanted to stay in the game of frontier models, we couldn't just keep optimizing products on top of a model that wasn't at the frontier. So the question wasn't really "should we train a trillion-parameter model," it was "do we accept that we will fall behind if we don't." Framed that way, the decision was almost forced. What made it hard was the cost, the risk, and the fact that we were a relatively small team compared to the labs we'd be measured against.

But a decision like that is only meaningful if the technical groundwork is already there. You can't decide to train a very large model and then start figuring out how. The preparation came first, and in some sense it created the possibility of the decision.

Concretely, the most important piece was the optimizer. We had been working on Muon for a long time before K2, first at small scale, then scaling it up step by step. A trillion-parameter run at that level of compute is something you get to attempt roughly once, so the thing you are most afraid of is instability—a loss spike that ruins weeks of compute. We had to understand why Muon could become unstable at scale, which led to the clipping techniques, and we had to verify across many scaling-law experiments that the gains at small scale actually carried over. Only after we had that confidence could we say, "we can take this bet with an optimizer nobody has used at this size."

The second piece was data. Token efficiency matters enormously when your compute budget is constrained. You can't just throw more data at the problem; you have to get more learning out of every token. So the data pipeline, the rephrasing work, the way we constructed the mixture—all of that was being built in parallel, and a lot of it only paid off at the largest scale.

The third was infrastructure and the whole system around the run: sparsity choices, the MoE configuration, checkpointing, how to monitor the run so that if something went wrong we'd know early. Boring compared to the model itself, but it's what lets you sleep at night.

So I'd say the relationship is that the preparation turned an unreasonable decision into a reasonable one. If we'd made the same decision a year earlier, we probably would have failed, because the pieces weren't mature. And if we'd done all the preparation but then hesitated on the decision, the preparation would have been wasted. Scaling works, but scaling things that are unproven is how you burn resources. So we tried to scale only what we had already proven, and then be decisive about it.

There's also a cultural point. A small team can't afford many experiments at the largest scale, so you have to compensate by being more rigorous at smaller scales. That discipline—being willing to spend a long time on small experiments before committing—is itself part of the technical preparation. In a way, the decision to train K2 was really a decision to trust the experiments we had already run.

r001.rationale: The response says the technical preparation had to come first and that an earlier decision likely would have failed, but it does not state that starting the groundwork after the decision would make training K2 within two or three months infeasible.

astra-6.text:
I think the decision and the technical preparation are closely connected, but they’re not the same thing. You can decide that you want to train K2, but that doesn’t mean you’re ready to do it. You still need confidence that the approach will work and that the team can execute it.

At the same time, preparation doesn’t happen entirely before the decision. You need a direction to decide which problems to work on. So I see it as an iterative process: the ambition guides the preparation, and what you learn during preparation makes the decision more concrete. The key is knowing which uncertainties you need to resolve before committing and which you can resolve along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says the team needs technical preparation before it is ready, but it does not state that training K2 within two or three months would be infeasible if the groundwork started from scratch after the decision.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the decision to train K2 and the technical preparation were closely connected. It wasn’t simply a matter of deciding to do it and then figuring out how. You need enough technical evidence to believe that scaling up is worthwhile. At the same time, committing to a model gives the research a concrete target: which uncertainties have to be resolved, which capabilities matter most, and what has to be reliable before training begins.

So I would describe it as an iterative process. Preparation makes the decision possible, and the decision helps focus the remaining preparation. You don’t need every question answered, but you do need a clear understanding of the major risks and why you’re ready to take them.

r001.rationale: The response says technical evidence and preparation help make the decision possible, but it does not state that training K2 within two or three months would be infeasible if groundwork began only after the decision.
